title: Global development progress is slowing unevenly as work, poverty, infrastructure, and digital access diverge by place
source_unit: World Bank, Atlas of Global Development 2026
geography: Global country comparisons across people, prosperity, planet, infrastructure, and digital transformation

denominator.unit: development indicators explored in the World Bank Atlas

slowest_progress.unit: indicators where progress is at its slowest on record

progress_frame.value: the Atlas tracks how quickly countries move toward better outcomes from their own starting points

time_horizon.unit: years of development progress tracked in the new framework

observations.method: World Bank interactive data storytelling using cross-country indicators and historical development series.
observations.uncertainty: Indicator coverage, starting points, missing data, and aggregation affect comparisons; speed of progress does not establish a single cause or imply equal lived experience within countries.
observations.subgroup: Countries at different starting points, slower-progress regions, policymakers, households, workers, and communities facing stalled development outcomes.
observations.counterinterpretation: A slowdown in aggregate progress can coexist with rapid improvement in particular countries or domains, making differentiated policy and place-sensitive comparison important.

denominator.unit: global working-age population and gender-work comparison frame

women_income_generating_work.unit: approximate share of women engaged in income-generating work

work_barriers.value: women face persistent barriers to work, are more likely to be in vulnerable jobs, and earn lower wages

care_burden.value: women shoulder a disproportionate care burden

skills_channel.value: schooling and on-the-job learning both contribute to productivity and wages

observations.method: Cross-country development indicators and World Bank synthesis of gender, jobs, learning, productivity, and wages.
observations.uncertainty: The summary is not a causal estimate of care, education, or labor-market effects and does not identify individual work histories or within-household allocation.
observations.subgroup: Women, workers in vulnerable jobs, caregivers, young people, employers, and countries with large gender gaps in labor-market participation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Skills investment, care infrastructure, labor protections, and reduced barriers can change both participation and job quality; current gaps are not fixed outcomes.

denominator.unit: global extreme-poverty and country-development comparison frame

poor_in_stalled_countries.unit: approximate share of the world's extreme poor living in countries where poverty increased over the past decade

regional_gap.value: the prosperity gap in sub-Saharan Africa is at a level comparable to the world in the 1980s, roughly four decades behind the global average

policy_route.value: combining income growth with inequality reduction benefits everyone

observations.method: World Bank cross-country poverty, prosperity, inequality, and historical development comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: Country-level aggregates conceal local mobility, household resources, informal economies, and differences in price levels and distribution; the comparison is not a household panel.
observations.subgroup: People in extreme poverty, residents of countries with rising poverty, sub-Saharan African communities, workers, and households with limited economic room.
observations.counterinterpretation: Place-based progress, redistribution, human-capital investment, and economic growth can jointly reduce poverty rather than forcing a choice between growth and equity.

denominator.unit: global infrastructure, service access, and digital inclusion frame

water_quality.unit: countries with data, out of 94, facing water-quality challenges

electricity_sub_saharan_africa.unit: approximate share of people in sub-Saharan Africa living without electricity

internet_nonuse.unit: approximate share of people worldwide who do not use the Internet

digital_divide.value: lower-income countries face infrastructure and skills gaps in access to and exposure to artificial intelligence

observations.method: Cross-country infrastructure and digital-access indicators presented through the World Bank Atlas thematic stories.
observations.uncertainty: Access statistics do not fully measure reliability, affordability, quality, use, skills, or household-level control; country averages can hide rural and urban divides.
observations.subgroup: Rural communities, low-income countries, households without electricity or safe water, nonusers of the Internet, and workers exposed to digital skill gaps.
observations.counterinterpretation: Targeted infrastructure investment, affordability policy, maintenance, skills development, and public accountability can convert access expansion into usable capability.

related_sources.claim: World Development Indicators provide the underlying global development indicator context.
World Bank Data360 provides the interactive data platform supporting the Atlas.

boundary: This record adds a cross-domain global-development, gender-work, poverty-geography, infrastructure-access, and digital-divide route. It uses World Bank indicator comparisons and report-level synthesis, not respondent-level records, individual income histories, household time diaries, causal infrastructure estimates, or proof that country-level progress translates evenly into lived experience.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank Atlas page reviewed for the five-theme framework, 26-indicator progress summary, 75-year comparison frame, gender and work, poverty geography, water quality, electricity, Internet use, and digital-gap findings.
